title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.

source_formulation.text: Determine whether exact equivalence of nondeterministic discounted-sum automata over infinite words is decidable.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

why: Exact equivalence is a basic correctness test for quantitative specifications: it asks whether replacing one finite-state description by another preserves the value of every possible infinite behavior. Discounting makes each value convergent but leaves a difficult interaction between exact arithmetic and nondeterministic choices. Resolving equivalence for the basic rational single-factor model would establish a central algorithmic boundary for quantitative automata.
status_note: Source-open for general total nondeterministic automata over infinite words with one shared rational factor. Checked the CONCUR 2023 open statement and LICS 2024 comparison scope, followed by the 2025 LMCS multiple-factor results, the November 2025 revised target-sum paper, and a September 2026 probabilistic preprint. No matching general resolution was found in this bounded review on 15 September 2026. New preprints and cited proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The CONCUR paper defines the supremum semantics in §2 and explicitly leaves discounted-sum equivalence open in §3. Its Theorem 3.3 proves PSPACE-completeness of deciding whether a discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function.

Boker’s LICS 2024 Theorems 5.4–5.5 give decidability for Pisot divisor discount factors and suitable algebraic weights. In particular this includes integer divisors, hence reciprocal-integer multipliers here; it does not cover arbitrary rational multipliers.
The LMCS paper proves equivalence undecidable for a model allowing different integral divisor factors on different transitions. A single common rational multiplier is not that model.

The revised target discounted-sum manuscript gives positive results for functional automata over finite words in §6. Its word domain and restricted run values differ from the present general infinite-word problem.

A preprint on target discounted sums computes probabilities for finite Markov chains and studies related strategy objectives. These probabilistic questions do not provide a pointwise equivalence algorithm for the automata here.

importance.reason: Equivalence is a foundational comparison problem for quantitative languages and a prerequisite for certified model replacement. The open general rational-discount case persists despite decidable deterministic, integral-base and other structured fragments, exposing a substantial arithmetic and nondeterministic boundary.
importance.basis: Individual assessment from the CONCUR 2023 statement, LICS 2024 comparison results and checked 2025–2026 work.

sentences: A discounted-sum automaton assigns a convergent weighted value to each infinite run, with later weights geometrically discounted.
Its value on an infinite word is the supremum over all runs carrying that word.
The question asks for exact decidability of equality of two such functions for every input rational discount factor shared by the automata.
Known results for constant functions, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words and transition-dependent discounting have different scopes.
A resolution would determine whether arbitrary nondeterministic quantitative specifications in this basic model can be compared algorithmically.

definitions: Such an automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,q_0,\Sigma,E,\gamma)\), where \(Q\) is a finite nonempty state set, \(q_0\in Q\), \(E\) is a finite set of transitions with source, target and label in \(Q,Q,\Sigma\), and \(\gamma:E\to\mathbb Q\) gives their weights. Parallel transitions, including differently weighted transitions with the same endpoints and label, are allowed. Totality means that every pair \((q,a)\in Q\times\Sigma\) has at least one outgoing transition. There are no empty-label transitions, final-state tests, fairness requirements or restrictions on which infinite runs count. For an infinite word \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run \(\rho=e_0e_1\cdots\) starts at \(q_0\), consecutive transitions have matching endpoints, and \(e_i\) has label \(a_i\). Set \[\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i\gamma(e_i),\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\sup_{\rho\text{ a run of }\mathcal A\text{ on }w}\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho).\] If \(W=\max_{e\in E}|\gamma(e)|\), every series converges absolutely and has absolute value at most \(W/(1-\lambda)\); totality ensures a nonempty run set, so the supremum is a finite real number. Nondeterministic choices are optimized separately for each complete word. No single online strategy is required to select them. All finite sets and transition tables are explicit, and rational weights and the common multiplier \(\lambda\) are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. The deciding machine takes these finite descriptions, not an infinite word as an oracle input. It must answer correctly on every well-formed pair and every allowed factor, without a resource bound. Equality is exact equality of real-valued functions on all infinite words; this yes-or-no decidability question has no approximation tolerance.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one total computable algorithm decides the stated equality for every encoded input, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A positive result must handle arbitrary rational \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), unrestricted finite nondeterminism, signed rational weights and all infinite words under supremum semantics. A result for deterministic or functional automata, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words, or comparison up to a positive tolerance does not settle the full target. A negative result obtained by permitting different discount factors on different transitions does not settle this single-factor problem.

context_blocks.text: A transition weight represents a local reward or cost. Multiplication by successive powers of the discount factor gives later weights less influence. The automaton chooses the best run separately on each input word, producing a quantitative language rather than a set of accepted words. Equivalence compares those whole functions.

The source considers total automata, rational weights and supremum semantics on infinite words. Its shared value-function convention is made explicit by supplying one multiplier for both automata. Some papers instead divide the weight at position \(i\) by \(\beta^i\), with \(\beta>1\), and take infima; their discount corresponds to \(\lambda=1/\beta\), and negating all weights interchanges the two extremum conventions.

Convergence does not turn exact function equality into a test of finitely many sampled behaviors or fixed-precision values. The 2023 paper can decide whether one discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function while explicitly leaving arbitrary equivalence open. Constancy is a special case and does not give the required pairwise comparison procedure.

Later results depend sharply on the model. Reciprocal-integer multipliers belong to a decidable family, and more general real-valued Pisot-base results extend that family outside the rational domain. Conversely, undecidability with transition-dependent discount factors concerns a richer interface. Neither result settles all rational multipliers shared throughout a pair of nondeterministic automata.
